newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk police in rare trial for journalist killing.
newsitem.headline: Turk police in rare trial for journalist killing.

text.p: Forty-eight Turkish police go on trial on Friday for the beating to death of a leftist journalist in a rare human rights case under the critical eye of Ankara's European allies and Western rights groups.

"This case has the potential to be a step in the right direction or a nail in the coffin (for Turkey)," said a Western diplomat, referring to Turkey's ties with the European Union -- a group it is struggling to join amid rights and other concerns.
Eleven police have been charged with the fatal beating of Metin Goktepe while in custody in January. The others face various charges for indirect involvement.

Claims of extrajudicial killings and deaths by torture in Turkish police custody are rife -- the Ankara-based Human Rights Association says there were 21 just in August this year -- but it is rare that the perpetrators come before the law.

"At this time it must be remembered that the state has not begun any investigation into the killing since 1988 of 20 journalists on duty," the independent Reporters Sans Frontieres (RSF) group said in a statement.

"This is a very important case -- if it is proved that he was killed by police it is a case of extrajudicial killing and a serious human rights case. I wish all such cases could came to court," Jose Herrero of Amnesty International told Reuters.
Turkey's human rights record has long been under fire from Europe, and almost derailed plans for a customs union deal with the EU that eventually went into effect in January.

Its critics slam Ankara for systematic torture during detentions, extrajudicial killings, bad prison conditions, harsh restrictions on expression, rough crack-downs against civil protest and a heavy-handed approach to a 12-year Kurdish insurgency in the southeast, which is under emergency rule.
Rights activists say after customs union Turkey, which changed some of its criticised legislation ahead of the deal, stopped trying to impress the west and condoned further abuses.

The wide use of tracking people under its laws that restrict expression has continued. This week a musician and leading rights activist was arrested for writing the music for a programme broadcast on a Kurdish channel based outside Turkey.
RSF said it had sent a delegation to Aydin to observe the Goktepe trial. Members of the European Parliament -- a strong critic of Turkey's rights situation -- would also be there.
Inside Turkey, the excitement of seeing the case come to court at last is dampened by the length of time it took to be processed and pessimism the trial will not be fair.

"Despite the fact that 282 days have passed since he was killed by police, Metin's killers are coming before the law for the first time on Friday," said the leftist daily Evrensel, where Goktepe was working as a reporter when he was detained.

"I don't expect a positive result," Goktepe's brother Ibrahim told Evrensel. "If the people owning up to Metin's death for show had actually been responsible for it this thing would have been solved before and the murderers would be punished."

The case has been transferred from Istanbul, where the incident took place, to the western town of Aydin for security reasons. None of the accused are under arrest and they are not expected to be present at Friday's hearing. All statements for both the prosecution and the defence will be taken out of court.
"The court won't see anyone and directives for more questions will fly back and fourth. At this rate, the trail will last 10 years," said Leyla Han, lawyer for Goktepe's family.
